**What you should be able to do after this meeting.** Say which AI modality suits which job, and why. Interrogate a real dataset through one, and catch something wrong with it before it reaches your proposal.

## Where to read more

[Adams](https://doi.org/10.4135/9788132108498) ch. 11 on descriptive analysis — what to compute first, and what it tells you.

## Session A · 2:05–3:15

First, the modalities. 'Use AI' is four different things. Chat answers from memory, and will invent a citation. File upload with code execution writes and runs real code on your data, so the output is checkable. Retrieval answers from documents you supplied. Agents act over several steps, and compound a mistake made early. The one you want here is the second, and knowing why is the point. Then the harder half, which is the whole skill in this course: knowing whether an answer is right without reading the code that produced it. Row counts across a join. Totals checked against a published figure. Five raw records read by hand. Orders of magnitude. And what you must not upload, and why.

## Session B · 3:35–4:30

Every session B opens with a ten-minute team check-in: what you did
since last week, what is stuck, and who is doing what next. Written
down, and handed in with that session's work.

Real data in front of you, and the meeting-9 checklist put to work: what is one row, how many are there, what is missing, what changed over time. Every dataset handed out has something wrong with it. Find it, then say which check would have caught it — that second half is the graded one. Then the same move on your own project's data. Whatever you cannot answer about it today is what you chase before the outline is due.

Your team's output is submitted before you leave.
